For example, $$ \textrm E[2X+5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] + 5 \textrm E[Y]. $$ Note that the property also works with subtraction: $$ \textrm E[2X-5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] - 5 \textrm E[Y] $$ We can extend this idea to any number of random variables. For example, for any random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ and real constants $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$, we have $$ \textrm{E}[a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\cdots+ a_nX_n]= a_1\textrm E[X_1]+a_2\textrm E[X_2]+\cdots +a_n\textrm{E}[X_n], $$ or more concisely, $$ \textrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \textrm E[X_i]. $$ Note that the random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ are *not* required to be independent." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186173187 :tutorial/content "The expected value of the product of two *independent* random variables is equal to the product of the expected values. $$

$$

$$

> For any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b$, we have

In other words, the expected value of a sum of scaled random variables equals the sum of the scaled expected values.

For example,

$$
\textrm E[2X+5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] + 5 \textrm E[Y]
$$

Note that the property also works with subtraction:

$$
\textrm E[2X-5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] - 5 \textrm E[Y]
$$

We can extend this idea to any number of random variables. For example, for any random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$, and real constants $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$, we have

$$

$$

or more concisely,

$$
\textrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \textrm E[X_i]
$$
